# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. The pilot week saw 160 boardings, rising to 240 the following week, but these figures track trips rather than unique students [@lyra:1]. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase indicates higher service utilization without proving a causal effect on class presence. The counts suggest someone used the service more often, yet they do not tell me whether more students came to class.

-My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+The boarding counts establish utilization but leave the broader demand question open. The accompanying survey collected responses exclusively from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses cannot indicate how many students outside the pilot would choose the service if it expanded. This representativeness gap means the current data describe existing riders rather than potential ones. The evidence therefore supports a need for more careful measurement that includes student voices beyond those already on the bus, rather than a final policy decision based on partial input.

+Given these limits, I recommend extending the pilot for one term, contingent on improved data collection. The utilization gap identified in the evidence section means we cannot yet confirm that increased access raised class participation. Extending the trial is not a declaration of success; it is a mechanism to resolve this uncertainty. The next term must distinguish between ridership volume and actual student engagement with coursework. Without this step, we risk treating a transportation log as an academic metric. The proposal is conditional on implementing the measurement changes detailed below, ensuring the extension serves investigative purposes rather than cementing an unverified success narrative.

+Concretely, the extended term’s data collection must reach non-riders, a group the current survey entirely skipped [@lyra:2]. Instead of asking only those who chose the shuttle why they do, we should ask students who do not ride about their specific barriers and preferences [@lyra:2]. This direct input allows us to see the service from the perspective of those who exclude it, rather than inferring demand from the few who use it [@lyra:2]. Furthermore, because the pilot did not collect cost or emissions data [@lyra:2], we should not fabricate financial or environmental benefits. By restricting our analysis to observed usage and stated accessibility, we keep the investigation honest and avoid treating missing information as proof of either success or failure.

## Evidence

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. The pilot week saw 160 boardings, rising to 240 the following week, but these figures track trips rather than unique students [@lyra:1]. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase indicates higher service utilization without proving a causal effect on class presence. The counts suggest someone used the service more often, yet they do not tell me whether more students came to class.

The boarding counts establish utilization but leave the broader demand question open. The accompanying survey collected responses exclusively from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses cannot indicate how many students outside the pilot would choose the service if it expanded. This representativeness gap means the current data describe existing riders rather than potential ones. The evidence therefore supports a need for more careful measurement that includes student voices beyond those already on the bus, rather than a final policy decision based on partial input.

## Recommendation

Given these limits, I recommend extending the pilot for one term, contingent on improved data collection. The utilization gap identified in the evidence section means we cannot yet confirm that increased access raised class participation. Extending the trial is not a declaration of success; it is a mechanism to resolve this uncertainty. The next term must distinguish between ridership volume and actual student engagement with coursework. Without this step, we risk treating a transportation log as an academic metric. The proposal is conditional on implementing the measurement changes detailed below, ensuring the extension serves investigative purposes rather than cementing an unverified success narrative.

Concretely, the extended term’s data collection must reach non-riders, a group the current survey entirely skipped [@lyra:2]. Instead of asking only those who chose the shuttle why they do, we should ask students who do not ride about their specific barriers and preferences [@lyra:2]. This direct input allows us to see the service from the perspective of those who exclude it, rather than inferring demand from the few who use it [@lyra:2]. Furthermore, because the pilot did not collect cost or emissions data [@lyra:2], we should not fabricate financial or environmental benefits. By restricting our analysis to observed usage and stated accessibility, we keep the investigation honest and avoid treating missing information as proof of either success or failure.

live_draft_suggestions.base_content:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. The pilot week saw 160 boardings, rising to 240 the following week, but these figures track trips rather than unique students [@lyra:1]. Because no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase indicates higher service utilization without proving a causal effect on class presence. The counts suggest someone used the service more often, yet they do not tell me whether more students came to class.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: The boarding counts establish utilization but leave the broader demand question open. The accompanying survey collected responses exclusively from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these responses cannot indicate how many students outside the pilot would choose the service if it expanded. This representativeness gap means the current data describe existing riders rather than potential ones. The evidence therefore supports a need for more careful measurement that includes student voices beyond those already on the bus, rather than a final policy decision based on partial input.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Given these limits, I recommend extending the pilot for one term, contingent on improved data collection. The utilization gap identified in the evidence section means we cannot yet confirm that increased access raised class participation. Extending the trial is not a declaration of success; it is a mechanism to resolve this uncertainty. The next term must distinguish between ridership volume and actual student engagement with coursework. Without this step, we risk treating a transportation log as an academic metric. The proposal is conditional on implementing the measurement changes detailed below, ensuring the extension serves investigative purposes rather than cementing an unverified success narrative.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Concretely, the extended term’s data collection must reach non-riders, a group the current survey entirely skipped [@lyra:2]. Instead of asking only those who chose the shuttle why they do, we should ask students who do not ride about their specific barriers and preferences [@lyra:2]. This direct input allows us to see the service from the perspective of those who exclude it, rather than inferring demand from the few who use it [@lyra:2]. Furthermore, because the pilot did not collect cost or emissions data [@lyra:2], we should not fabricate financial or environmental benefits. By restricting our analysis to observed usage and stated accessibility, we keep the investigation honest and avoid treating missing information as proof of either success or failure.
